chief_complaint: recurrent mild RUQ pain and gallstones on ultrasound
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with recurrent mild ruq pain and gallstones on ultrasound. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the gallstones detected on her ultrasound are shifting and irritating her liver after heavy meals.
concerns: She is worried that her gallbladder will suddenly burst and require emergency open surgery right before her daughter's wedding.
expectations: She hopes to get medication that can dissolve the stones so she can avoid having surgery altogether.

available_results.value: Multiple gallstones with a contracted mildly thick-walled gallbladder; no pericholecystic fluid, biliary duct dilatation, or sonographic Murphy sign

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Cholecystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management for Chronic Cholecystitis emphasizes referral for elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with recurrent mild ruq pain and gallstones on ultrasound. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Chronic Cholecystitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Cholecystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute cholecystitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden worsening pain with fever — suggests acute cholecystitis.
management_principles: Plan for Chronic Cholecystitis: Refer for elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of recurrent mild RUQ pain and gallstones on ultrasound, consistent with chronic gallbladder wall inflammation.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Chronic Cholecystitis.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Chronic Cholecystitis: Refer for elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

teaching.one_liner: Recurrent low-grade gallbladder inflammation from chronic gallstone irritation, causing mild, recurring RUQ pain rather than a single acute attack.
red_flags: Sudden worsening pain with fever — suggests acute cholecystitis

must_ask.say: Does the pain come and go over months, rather than being one bad attack?
Does it happen after fatty meals?
How severe is the pain compared to before?
Have you been told you have gallstones on an ultrasound?
Have you ever had fever with any of these episodes?

history.answer: I have been having recurring mild pain in my upper right belly, and an ultrasound showed gallstones.
It started a few months ago and has been gradually happening more often.
The ache is right in my upper right belly, and it stays in that exact spot without moving around.
It does not spread to my shoulder, back, or groin.
It feels like a dull, heavy ache or pressure rather than a sharp stabbing pain.
On a scale of one to ten, it is about a three or four, and an episode usually lasts one to two hours before fading.
It usually flares up an hour after I eat, especially if the meal was heavy or greasy. Resting quietly helps it pass.
Yes, I have had several similar episodes of this mild ache over the past few months.
My local clinic did an abdominal ultrasound last week and told me I have multiple gallstones and a thickened gallbladder.
I have been feeling more worn out and sluggish than usual over the past couple of weeks.
I feel slightly queasy sometimes when the ache starts, but I haven't thrown up at all.
My bowel movements have been completely regular, with no diarrhea, constipation, or blood.
No, I have not had any fever, sweating, or chills.
No, my eyes and skin haven't turned yellow, my urine looks normal, and my stool is a normal brown.
I have no pain or burning when urinating, and I haven't noticed any frequent urination or blood.
No, I have not felt lightheaded, dizzy, or faint.
No, I have had no vaginal bleeding or unusual discharge.
No, I have had no chest tightness, chest pain, or shortness of breath.
Eating fried chicken, pork belly, or other oily foods definitely brings on the discomfort. I only have a drink occasionally.
No, I haven't taken any aspirin, ibuprofen, or other pain relievers for this.
No, I have never had an irregular heartbeat, atrial fibrillation, or blood vessel problems.
I figured the gallstones they found on my scan are just sliding around and irritating my liver whenever I eat.
I'm really worried this will turn into an emergency and need open surgery right before my daughter's wedding next month.
I was hoping you could give me pills to dissolve these stones so I won't need to go under the knife.
I don't have any chronic illnesses like hypertension, diabetes, or liver disease.
I have never had any surgeries or stays in the hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink half a glass of wine on special social occasions, maybe once every few months.
I am a retired teacher and live comfortably with my husband.
My mother had her gallbladder taken out for gallstones, but there are no other illnesses in the family.
I went through menopause more than ten years ago, so pregnancy is not possible.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and temperature 36.6°C.
Alert, comfortable, and in no acute distress.
Sclerae are anicteric and conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended with no surgical scars.
Normal active bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants with no bruits.
Mild deep tenderness on palpation in the right upper quadrant, but the abdomen remains soft without involuntary guarding.
No rebound tenderness or peritoneal signs noted.
Negative Murphy sign with no inspiratory arrest during deep palpation of the right subcostal margin.
No tenderness at McBurney's point, and negative psoas and obturator signs.
